tier_reason: Peer-reviewed SIGMOD 2020 paper (Section 5.2, Figure 14) shows the Crystal GPU implementation beating OmniSci, a commercial GPU OLAP DBMS, by about 16x on average on SSB on the same V100. It stays below A because the repo (src/ssb/*.cu plus Makefile) holds only the GPU queries: the CPU implementation and the OmniSci/Hyper/MonetDB runs are not scripted, and the CPU build flags are unstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Per the SIGMOD 2020 paper (Section 5.2): the Crystal-based Standalone GPU implementation is on average about 16x faster than OmniSci (a commercial GPU OLAP DBMS) on the same V100, and on average 25x faster than the authors' own equivalent CPU implementation across the 13 SSB queries. The 1.17x (vs Hyper) and 2.5x (vs MonetDB) averages belong to the authors' Standalone CPU implementation, not to Crystal on the GPU. The paper does not state direct GPU-vs-Hyper or GPU-vs-MonetDB ratios.
corrections.baseline: OmniSci (commercial GPU OLAP DBMS, formerly MapD, now HEAVY.AI) on the same GPU. Also the authors' own equivalent CPU implementation, which is itself compared against Hyper and MonetDB.
corrections.workload: 13 Star Schema Benchmark queries at scale factor 20 (120M-row lineorder fact table, about 13 GB). String columns are dictionary-encoded to 4-byte integers and the queries are manually rewritten. Data is preloaded into device memory, and each result is the average of 3 runs. Crystal on the GPU (thread block 256, 8 items per thread per tile) is compared with OmniSci on the GPU and with an equivalent CPU implementation; Hyper and MonetDB are compared only with that CPU implementation.
corrections.hardware: CPU: single-socket Intel i7-6900 (the paper calls it Skylake-class; 8 cores/16 SMT, AVX2, 64 GB). GPU: Nvidia V100 (32 GB, 880 GB/s; measured bidirectional PCIe 12.8 GB/s). Ubuntu 16.04, CUDA 10.0.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GPU: nvcc (CUDA 10.0). The repo Makefile compiles with -O3 --std=c++11 -Xptxas="-dlcm=cg" and defaults to gencode sm_52 (the sm_70 lines are commented out). CPU-implementation compiler and flags are not stated.
corrections.caveats: The headline GPU speedups are largely cross-hardware: a V100 against an 8-core desktop CPU, a memory-bandwidth ratio of about 16x. The paper is a GPU-vs-CPU study; the like-for-like incumbent comparison is Crystal vs OmniSci on the same GPU (about 16x). Hyper and MonetDB were compared only against the authors' CPU implementation. The CPU implementation and the baseline-system runs are not in the repo. The ~13 GB SF20 dataset fits in GPU memory. Published at SIGMOD 2020, so it predates DuckDB/ClickHouse-era baselines. The last commit on master (the only branch) is 2020-08-29; the 2024-06-03 date is GitHub's pushed_at, not a commit. It is an academic reference library.

notes: The record's claimed_speedup misreads the paper: 2.5x and 1.17x are the authors' CPU code vs MonetDB/Hyper, and '>5x' refers to Peloton being slower. The real Crystal numbers are larger (about 16x vs OmniSci, 25x vs CPU). The tier stays B. last_commit/maintenance are fixed from 2024 'stale' to 2020 'abandoned'.

tier_reason: The arXiv paper by LanceDB authors compares Lance 2.1 random access against tuned parquet-rs on stated hardware (i7-10700K, Samsung 970 EVO Plus). In the text it reports only that Lance 'generally tie[s] or beat[s] Parquet', with no stated ratio. The 100x headline comes only from first-party README/homepage copy without methodology. Peer review (VLDB '25) is claimed by the project homepage but could not be confirmed, and neither compiler/flags nor a linked script path is given, so the tier is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README/homepage marketing: '100x faster random access than Parquet or Iceberg'. The README's 'Vs. parquet' section attributes this to a preliminary Oxford Pet dataset test ('For batched random access, Lance is 100x better than both parquet and raw files'). The paper (arXiv 2504.15247) states instead that Parquet 'when configured correctly, can achieve over 60x better random access performance than default settings' (parquet-rs default 5,500 rows/s vs optimized 350,000 rows/s on small scalars). It also says the Lance 2.1 encoding 'generally tie[s] or beat[s] Parquet' in random access without the scan-performance and RAM trade-offs, but gives no single speedup figure against tuned Parquet.
corrections.baseline: Apache Parquet (the parquet-rs Rust crate, tuned, in the paper). Iceberg is named only in the README/homepage marketing and is not benchmarked in the paper.
corrections.workload: Paper (arXiv 2504.15247): parallel 'take' operations of 256 random indices from a single column, run for 10 s and reported as rows fetched per second, over 8 data types (UInt64 scalars through 100 KiB image lists) with 10% nulls. Small types use about 1 billion rows. Parquet uses 8 KiB pages with compression and dictionary encoding off. Full-scan, compression-ratio and struct-packing experiments are also included. All runs are on local NVMe.
corrections.hardware: Samsung 970 EVO Plus 2TB NVMe drive (measured 850K random 4KiB reads/s, 3,400 MiB/s) with an Intel i7-10700K CPU (8 cores/16 threads), per the paper
corrections.caveats: The '100x faster than Parquet or Iceberg' figure comes from README/homepage copy, backed only by a 'preliminary' Oxford Pet dataset test without methodology. The paper, written by LanceDB employees, undercuts it by showing tuned Parquet recovers over 60x versus default Parquet, and it claims only tie-or-beat against tuned Parquet. Lance 2.1 slightly underperforms Lance 2.0 on simple scalar types. The project homepage says the paper was published at VLDB 2025, but arXiv v1 carries no journal reference and a crossref title search found no match, so peer review is unconfirmed. The paper mentions reproduction scripts but gives no link. The paper's metric is throughput (rows/s) rather than latency.

notes: Metadata is confirmed: Apache-2.0, 7,117 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, not a fork. The record's 'metric: latency' is really throughput (rows/s) in the paper; metric is not a correctable field. The tier stays C.

tier_reason: These are first-party vendor numbers. The 2023 blog verbatim says 'ClickHouse has a response time 2.2x slower than that of StarRocks' on 13 SSB flat-table queries, with no hardware. The current StarRocks docs page reports 1.87x with instance types, versions and per-query latencies, but gives no CPU model, compiler/flags or public benchmark script, so it is C, not A/B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: StarRocks docs (SSB Flat-table Benchmarking): on 13 queries over the 100 GB SSB-Flat dataset, 'StarRocks has an overall query performance 1.87x that of ClickHouse' (sum of average latencies 992 ms vs 1,858 ms; per-query ratios 1.12x-2.63x). The earlier StarRocks blog post (Aug 21, 2023; https://www.starrocks.io/blog/benchmark-test) claimed 'ClickHouse has a response time 2.2x slower than that of StarRocks' on the same 13 SSB flat-table queries, with no hardware stated.
corrections.workload: Star Schema Benchmark flattened into a single wide table (SSB-Flat, 100 GB; the ClickHouse-style denormalized SSB, so no joins), 13 queries, 1 warm-up plus the average of 3 runs. StarRocks 3.5.0 vs ClickHouse 25.3.3.42 (and Apache Druid 33.0.0), all with default configurations.
corrections.hardware: AWS m7i.4xlarge hosts (16 vCPU, 64 GiB each; 5 instances listed). StarRocks runs 1 FE + 3 BEs and ClickHouse 3 nodes. CPU model and OS not stated.
corrections.caveats: These are vendor-run numbers: default configs, no CPU model, no compiler flags and no linked benchmark scripts. The 2023 blog gave 2.2x; the current docs give 1.87x (StarRocks 3.5.0 vs ClickHouse 25.3.3.42). The claim is contradicted by the independent ClickBench suite on identical single-node c6a.4xlarge hardware. There, ClickHouse's 2026-09-26 run sums to 18.03 s (best of 3 across 43 queries) versus 44.47 s for StarRocks' 2026-09-07 run, so ClickHouse is about 2.5x faster (derived from page data: ClickHouse/ClickBench clickhouse/results/20260926/c6a.4xlarge.json vs starrocks/results/20260907/c6a.4xlarge.json). Both the vendor SSB-Flat test and ClickBench are single-flat-table workloads, not star-schema joins, so the gap cannot be put down to join handling. It more likely reflects cluster vs single-node setup, dataset and query mix, and tuning. The win should be treated as workload- and setup-specific.

notes: Both the 2023 blog's 2.2x and the ClickBench 18.03 s vs 44.47 s figures were verified. The record's caveat wrongly calls the vendor test 'star-schema joins': it is SSB flat tables. benchmark_url was switched to the current docs page, which states instance type, versions and per-query data (1.87x); the old blog is kept in claimed_speedup/caveats. The orchestrator may want to flag this as contested given the independent ClickBench reversal.
